# Carrow Bell Tower Handbook

## Ringing and upkeep

The Carrow tower has eight bells, and the ringing chamber is opened for practice on Thursday evenings at 19:30 sharp. New ringers learn on the back bell, the tenor-sized one at the end of the row, only after they have handled a rope on the practice rig for a month. A novice never rings with fewer than four experienced ringers in the chamber, and the tower captain stands behind them throughout and calls the stop before anyone is pulled off their feet.

The tenor bell weighs 740 kilograms and is rung by the strongest member of the band, who is rotated every season so that no one's shoulders are ruined by the weight and so that the knowledge of the heavy bell is shared around. The tenor's clapper is inspected every spring and the leather baldric that holds it is replaced when it has frayed to half its thickness, usually after about six years of regular ringing in the tower.

All the bells are rung down before a funeral or a wedding is held, and are chimed with the clappers tied for the mourners if the family asks for it. The tower captain keeps the booking diary in the ringing chamber, and a booking is not confirmed until the fee has been paid into the tower fund, which pays for the oil, the ropes, and the annual visit from the bell hanger from the foundry.

The ropes are renewed on a fixed cycle and the sallies are re-covered in wool when they go slick. The bearings are oiled in the first week of October, using the grey oil in the cupboard, one squirt for each bearing, and the old oil is wiped from the frame so it does not drip on the floor below. A bell that has gone stiff is reported at once, since a stiff bell can throw a ringer off the rope.
